prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A number of recently discovered protein structures incorporate a rather unexpected structural feature: a knot in the polypeptide backbone. These knots are extremely rare, but their occurrence is likely connected to protein function in as yet unexplored fashion. Our analysis of the complete Protein Data Bank reveals several new knots which, along with previously discovered ones, can shed light on such connections. In particular, we identify the most complex knot discovered to date in human ubiquitin hydrolase, and suggest that its entangled topology protects it against unfolding and degradation by the proteasome. Knots in proteins are typically preserved across species and sometimes even across kingdoms. However, we also identify a knot which only appears in some transcarbamylases while being absent in homologous proteins of similar structure. The emergence of the knot is accompanied by a shift in the enzymatic function of the protein. We suggest that the simple insertion of a short DNA fragment into the gene may suffice to turn an unknotted into a knotted structure in this protein.

Our analysis of the complete Protein Data Bank reveals several new knots which, together with previously identified examples, may shed light on these connections. However, we also identify a knot that appears only in certain transcarbamylases while being absent from homologous proteins with similar structures. outputs.L2: Several protein structures identified in recent studies contain an unusual architectural element: the polypeptide chain is tied into a knot. Although such knots occur only very rarely, their presence may be linked to protein activity in ways that have not yet been fully investigated. By examining the entire Protein Data Bank, we found several previously unreported knots that, together with known examples, may help clarify these relationships. Notably, we detected the most intricate knot found so far in human ubiquitin hydrolase and propose that this tangled arrangement may shield the protein from unfolding and from breakdown by the proteasome. Nevertheless, we also found a knot present only in certain transcarbamylases and missing from homologous proteins with comparable structures. The appearance of this knot coincides with a change in the protein’s enzymatic role. We propose that, in this case, inserting a short segment of DNA into the gene could be enough to convert an unknotted protein structure into a knotted one.
outputs.L3:
Some recently discovered protein structures have revealed that a small number of proteins contain rare knots in their polypeptide backbones. In these proteins, the amino acid chain does not simply fold into a compact three-dimensional shape; instead, part of the chain threads through a loop, creating a true topological knot. Although such structures are uncommon, their discovery has raised important questions about how proteins fold, why knots are retained during evolution, and whether knotting contributes to biological function.

A systematic analysis of the complete Protein Data Bank has identified several previously unknown knotted proteins. These findings expand the known range of protein knot types and provide new opportunities to investigate the relationship between backbone topology and molecular function. Because knots can influence protein stability, folding pathways, and resistance to mechanical or enzymatic unfolding, each newly identified example helps clarify whether knotting is merely a structural curiosity or an adaptive feature.

The most complex protein knot discovered to date was found in human ubiquitin hydrolase. This enzyme contains a deeply embedded knot in its polypeptide chain, making it unusually intricate compared with other known knotted proteins. One proposed explanation for this topology is that the knot helps protect the protein from unfolding and degradation by the proteasome. Since proteasomal degradation typically requires proteins to be unfolded and threaded into the proteasome core, a tightly knotted backbone could slow or obstruct this process, thereby increasing the protein’s stability or lifetime in the cell.

Protein knots also show notable evolutionary patterns. In many cases, knotted structures are conserved across related species, suggesting that they provide some functional or structural advantage. In a few instances, similar knots are preserved across much broader evolutionary distances, even across kingdoms of life. Such conservation implies that once a beneficial knot emerges, natural selection may maintain it over long periods because it contributes to the protein’s activity, stability, or regulation.

One particularly informative example occurs in certain transcarbamylase enzymes. A knot found only in some members of this enzyme family is associated with a shift in enzymatic function, suggesting a direct connection between knot formation and functional divergence. Evidence indicates that this knot may have arisen through the insertion of a short DNA fragment into the gene encoding the protein. This insertion could have altered the folding pathway of the protein, allowing the polypeptide chain to thread through itself and form a knot. The resulting structural change may then have contributed to the emergence of a new or modified enzymatic activity.

Together, these discoveries show that protein knots, while rare, are biologically significant. They offer insight into the complex relationship between protein sequence, folding, topology, evolution, and function. As more protein structures are solved and analyzed, additional knotted proteins may be discovered, helping researchers understand how such unusual architectures arise and why they are preserved in nature.
outputs.L4:
A comprehensive analysis of structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank was carried out to investigate the occurrence and significance of rare knots in protein backbones. Although most proteins fold into unknotted three-dimensional shapes, a small number contain true topological knots formed by the path of the polypeptide chain. These unusual structures are of particular interest because they raise important questions about how proteins fold, how such complicated architectures evolved, and whether knots provide functional advantages.

The study systematically examined known protein structures and identified several previously unrecognized knotted proteins. Among the most notable findings was the discovery of an exceptionally complex knot in a human ubiquitin hydrolase, representing the most intricate protein knot known at the time of analysis. Ubiquitin hydrolases are enzymes involved in removing ubiquitin tags from proteins, a process closely connected to protein degradation and cellular regulation. The presence of a deep and complex knot in such an enzyme suggests that knotting may influence protein stability, folding pathways, or resistance to unfolding and degradation.

The analysis also showed that protein knots are not randomly distributed. In many cases, knotted regions appear to be evolutionarily conserved, meaning that related proteins across different species retain similar knotted architectures. This conservation implies that the knots may serve important biological roles rather than being accidental structural features. A knot can potentially stabilize a protein’s active site, help maintain a precise three-dimensional arrangement required for catalysis, or protect key structural regions from mechanical or enzymatic breakdown.

In addition to structural and functional observations, the study explored how such knots might have evolved. One proposed mechanism is that short insertions in DNA, which add extra amino acid segments to a protein, can gradually create or deepen knots in the folded structure. These insertions may alter the protein’s topology while also producing changes in function. Over evolutionary time, if the resulting knotted structure provides an advantage—such as improved stability, altered substrate specificity, or protection from degradation—it may be retained and refined by natural selection.

Overall, the Protein Data Bank analysis suggests that knotted proteins, though rare, are biologically meaningful. The discovery of new knots, including the highly complex knot in human ubiquitin hydrolase, expands our understanding of the relationship between protein topology, evolution, and function. Rather than being structural curiosities, knots may represent specialized adaptations that help proteins perform demanding cellular roles, resist degradation, and evolve new functional properties.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a scientific paper about newly discovered knots in protein backbones and their possible functional significance.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Knots in protein backbones represent rare and topologically complex structural motifs whose origins and biological roles remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the identification of several previously unrecognized knotted protein structures through a systematic analysis of high-resolution protein models. Using topology-preserving backbone closure methods and knot classification algorithms, we detected new instances of deep and shallow knots spanning multiple protein families and folds. Structural comparisons indicate that these knots are not artifacts of modeling or chain closure, but stable features conserved in related sequences or supported by experimental density where available. Mapping of knotted regions onto functional annotations suggests that the entangled segments often occur near ligand-binding pockets, catalytic residues, oligomerization interfaces, or mechanically important domains. In several cases, the knot appears to constrain local geometry, stabilize active-site architecture, or influence conformational dynamics, implying a potential role in enhancing protein stability, regulating function, or guiding folding pathways. These findings expand the known repertoire of knotted proteins and support the view that backbone topology can contribute directly to molecular function. More broadly, our results highlight the importance of topological analysis in structural biology and provide new candidates for experimental studies of protein folding, stability, and evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize findings from a complete Protein Data Bank analysis identifying rare knotted protein structures, including ubiquitin hydrolase and transcarbamylases.
counterfactuals.output:
A complete survey of Protein Data Bank structures found that **true knots in proteins are extremely rare**, but a small number of robust, biologically meaningful examples do exist. The analysis used computational closure/simplification of protein backbones to distinguish genuine topological knots from superficial chain entanglements caused by termini or local geometry.

Key findings:

- **Knotted proteins are exceptional in the PDB.**  
  Only a tiny fraction of solved protein structures contained unambiguous knots, showing that evolution generally avoids heavily entangled backbone topologies.

- **Most detected knots were trefoil knots, but more complex knots were also found.**  
  The commonest protein knot was the **trefoil knot** \(3₁\), but the analysis also identified a rare **five-crossing knot**, notably in ubiquitin hydrolase.

- **Ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase contains a rare deep knot.**  
  Ubiquitin hydrolase structures, such as UCH-L proteins, were found to contain a **5₂ knot**, one of the most complex knots known in proteins. This knot is “deep,” meaning substantial portions of the chain must be removed from either terminus before the knot disappears.

- **Transcarbamylases also contain genuine knots.**  
  Several transcarbamylase enzymes, including members related to **ornithine transcarbamylase** and **N-acetylornithine transcarbamylase**, were identified as containing **trefoil-knotted backbones**. These knots are conserved within the family, suggesting they are not crystallographic accidents.

- **Knots tend to be conserved within structural families.**  
  When a knot was present in one representative of a protein family, related homologues often showed the same topology. This suggests that knotted folds arose early in evolution and were maintained.

- **Knots are usually associated with enzyme active-site architecture.**  
  Many knotted proteins are enzymes, and the knot often lies near or helps organize the active-site region. The topology may contribute to structural stability, substrate binding, or precise positioning of catalytic residues.

- **Protein knots are not random-polymer-like.**  
  Random compact polymers of similar length would be expected to knot much more frequently. The rarity of knots in natural proteins implies strong evolutionary and folding constraints against topological complexity.

- **Folding of knotted proteins poses a mechanistic challenge.**  
  These proteins must thread part of the chain through a loop during folding, or use stepwise folding pathways that effectively create the knot. Their existence shows that cellular folding machinery and protein energy landscapes can accommodate rare topological threading events.

Overall, the PDB-wide analysis showed that **knotted proteins are rare but real**, with notable examples including **ubiquitin hydrolase with a complex 5₂ knot** and **transcarbamylases with trefoil knots**. These structures demonstrate that protein evolution occasionally preserves intricate backbone topologies when they support stable or functional folds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise research abstract on the discovery of complex knots in proteins, their evolutionary conservation, and possible effects on degradation resistance and enzyme function.
counterfactuals.output: Complex knots in protein backbones represent rare but biologically significant topological features whose origins and functions remain incompletely understood. Recent structural surveys have identified deeply embedded and highly complex knots in diverse protein families, revealing that these motifs are not isolated anomalies but are often conserved across homologs and evolutionary lineages. Such conservation suggests that knotted architectures may confer selective advantages, despite the apparent folding challenges they impose. Proposed functional consequences include enhanced mechanical stability, reduced susceptibility to proteolytic degradation, and modulation of active-site geometry or conformational dynamics in enzymes. In several knotted enzymes, the knot core lies near catalytic or ligand-binding regions, indicating a potential role in maintaining precise structural arrangements required for activity. Comparative analyses further suggest that knot complexity can be preserved even when surrounding sequences diverge, supporting topology as an evolutionarily constrained feature. Understanding how complex protein knots arise, fold efficiently, and influence stability and catalysis will clarify their contribution to protein evolution and may guide the design of robust enzymes and biomaterials.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a journal-style abstract describing how protein backbone knots may relate to function, with examples involving human ubiquitin hydrolase and carbamyltransferase homologs.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Protein backbone knots, once considered rare structural curiosities, are increasingly recognized as potential contributors to protein function, regulation, and evolutionary diversification. By constraining global topology, knots can influence folding pathways, mechanical stability, ligand access, active-site architecture, and resistance to degradation. A prominent example is provided by human ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases, including UCH-L1 and related homologs, whose deeply embedded knot is positioned near structural elements that shape the catalytic cleft. In these enzymes, the knotted topology has been proposed to help organize the active-site environment and modulate substrate recognition, particularly for ubiquitin-linked substrates that require precise positioning for isopeptide-bond hydrolysis. The knot may also contribute to conformational rigidity or controlled flexibility, thereby coupling protein topology to enzymatic specificity and cellular regulation.

Comparable structure–function relationships are suggested by knotted carbamyltransferase homologs, in which conserved trefoil-like topologies occur near regions involved in oligomerization and substrate binding. In these enzymes, backbone entanglement may stabilize the fold around catalytic motifs, maintain the geometry of phosphate- and carbamyl-donor binding sites, or tune conformational changes associated with catalysis. Differences among homologs indicate that knots can be retained, modified, or lost during evolution while preserving related biochemical activities, suggesting that topology may act as an additional layer of functional constraint beyond sequence and local secondary structure.

Together, these examples support the view that protein knots are not merely accidental outcomes of folding but may be selectively maintained when they enhance stability, regulate dynamics, or reinforce active-site organization. Understanding how knotted backbones fold efficiently in vivo, how chaperones or cotranslational folding pathways assist their formation, and how topology affects catalytic performance remains an important challenge. Comparative studies of ubiquitin hydrolases, carbamyltransferases, and their unknotted homologs offer a valuable framework for linking protein topology to molecular function and evolutionary adaptation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a paragraph explaining recent discoveries of knotted protein structures, why they matter biologically, and how a small genetic insertion might create a knot in a protein.
counterfactuals.output: Recent discoveries have shown that protein knots—once thought to be rare curiosities—occur in a wider range of proteins than previously recognized, including enzymes and membrane-associated proteins whose chains thread through themselves in complex ways. These knotted structures matter biologically because a knot can affect how a protein folds, how stable it is, how resistant it is to degradation, and how its active site is positioned for function; in some cases, the knot may help protect an enzyme’s shape or regulate its interactions inside the cell. A small genetic insertion can create or deepen a knot by adding a short stretch of amino acids that changes the folding pathway or extends a loop near the protein’s end. During folding, one end of the protein chain may then pass through this loop before the structure locks into place, producing a topological knot even though the chemical sequence has changed only slightly.
